# Needs Review Assessment

Review date: 2026-09-24. Scope: all 285 files in [[Needs Review Inventory|Needs Review Inventory]] (126 reference notes and 159 category indexes).

This report records findings from the 2026-09-24 review snapshot. The 2026-09-25 migration applied the reviewed proposals: 280 inventory notes are now `Current`, five migrated references remain `Needs Review` pending checks, and the separate pre-existing Amazon ECS note also remains `Needs Review`. See [[Needs Review Migration Record|Needs Review Migration Record]] for current outcomes. The assessment below remains the evidence and findings history; its `Current gate` values describe the pre-migration snapshot. The earlier [[Knowledge Base Audit|Knowledge Base Audit]] supplies leads, not proof of current accuracy.

## Review criteria and outcomes

- **Accuracy:** Findings use `Supported`, `Partial`/`Partly supported`, `Unsupported`, `Stale`, `Ambiguous`, `Overbroad`, `Recommendation`, or `Unverified`/`Unverified-after-search` for scoped technical claims. `N/A` identifies nonmaterial candidate lines; `Recommendation` marks advice that needs context rather than a universal factual assertion. `Unverified-after-search` means exact evidence is still missing; it is not a pass. Source URLs and access date are recorded; publication or product version is included where checked. Other dated pages may still need metadata review. Recommendations give narrower or corrected wording for weak claims.
- **Detail:** The per-file finding explains whether the note gives a definition, use case, actionable guidance, a meaningful limit, and enough explanation or examples. For indexes, it assesses scope and navigation. No word-count threshold decides sufficiency.
- **KB rules:** The per-file finding checks required properties, title heading, sections, tags, links, and review schedule. Indexes must distinguish published notes from planned coverage and describe child categories. Filename/title differences and absent source URLs are editorial or evidence findings unless a specific rule requires them.
- **Location:** `Keep`, `Move proposed`, or `Clarify boundary`, with the approved taxonomy and nearby notes as context. An approved category with no published notes remains a valid location.
- **Current gate:** `Eligible`, `Not yet`, or `Unverified`. `Eligible` means the full file appears supportable against all criteria; this report makes no status change.

The read-only `Validate-KnowledgeBase.ps1 -Strict` baseline on the 2026-09-24 snapshot reported **0 errors and 0 warnings**. That check tests structural rules and links; it does not establish factual accuracy.

## Assessment summary

Each file has an accuracy, detail, KB-rule, location, action, and Current-gate outcome. **At the assessment snapshot, all 285 gates were `Not yet` and no file status had been promoted.** The report reviews all 126 reference notes. Its claim-level sections map 1,989 source-line candidates across all 126 notes: 965 in the first pass and 1,024 in the completeness pass. Supported verdicts do not override proposed edits. There were 269 explicitly unverified line findings (258 after search and 11 preliminary), plus 56 unsupported, 26 overbroad, 3 stale, and 1 ambiguous. Proposal changes were applied to their canonical notes; five references retain explicit execution/evidence checks. This migration did not include a fresh exhaustive fact-check of every sentence; see the migration record for remaining checks.

All external sources were accessed on 2026-09-24. An undated label means publication date was not recorded in this review; some dated pages still need metadata review. Source-note line numbers refer to this snapshot.

### Priority findings

1. Correct potentially misleading technical guidance first: synchronous `.Result` in an async cache example, EF Core InMemory testing advice, stale .NET 7 container examples, incorrect C# constraint and nullable guidance, and version-sensitive Azure messaging claims.
2. Substantiate or remove unsupported performance numbers and universal recommendations, including Entity Component System thresholds and database/product tuning claims.
3. Deepen notes that state a definition but lack a usable decision, example, or limit; add source links and dated review triggers where guidance is version-sensitive.
4. Keep approved taxonomy homes unless a separate location decision is justified. Clarify partial published/planned navigation and nearby category boundaries where the report flags them.

#### Areas/Foundations/Concurrency and Parallelism/Asynchronous Programming/Future and Promise.md
[[Future and Promise|Future and Promise]]
- **Accuracy:** **Partly supported.** Promise.all/Promise.race semantics match [ECMAScript 2025 specification](https://tc39.es/ecma262/2025/multipage/control-abstraction-objects.html); MDN [promises guide, publication date not shown](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Using_promises) documents browser microtask behavior. The future/promise read-versus-write split is a convention, not an ECMAScript or cross-language standard. Future versus promise is a useful convention, not universal language semantics. The later line checks support `TaskCompletionSource` and qualify `RunContinuationsAsynchronously`; terminology remains language-dependent.
- **Line-level accuracy update:** 24 candidates checked: 13 Partial, 11 Supported. See claim-level checks for sources and corrected wording; these later verdicts supersede provisional accuracy wording above.
- **Detail:** Good conceptual comparison and examples; distinguish eagerly started JavaScript promises from lazy future/task implementations and explain completion ownership.
- **KB rules:** Properties and required sections present; links resolve. Resource labels lack URLs.
- **Location:** **Keep** — cross-language async foundation, with language-specific links.
- **Actions:** Add the cited Java/C++ and .NET primary links to the note, qualify promise/future terminology, and make the continuation recommendation conditional.
- **Current gate:** **Not yet** until then.

#### Areas/Languages, Runtimes and Frameworks/Frameworks and Platforms/DotNET/Entity Framework Core/Performance/MemoryAllocations.md
[[MemoryAllocations|MemoryAllocations]]
- **Claim verdicts:** supported—entity tracking cost, DTO projection, `ToList` buffering, EF-internal buffering exceptions; partial—`AsNoTracking` in scalar DTO example; unverified—per-row closure/value tuple/struct/`ValueTask`/Span advice and comparative allocations; partial—`ToQueryString` exposes SQL but not a complete server/client computation trace.
- **Accuracy:** Partly supported. Projection, tracking only when entity instances are materialized, and possible internal buffering are supported by [EF tracking](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking) and [efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) (live EF Core docs, undated; accessed 2026-09-24). `AsNoTracking()` in the shown scalar DTO projection adds no tracking benefit because there is no entity instance. “Anonymous types may allocate” is broadly true but no measured comparison supports the value-tuple/struct advice. `ValueTask` and Span-backed parsing are not EF query allocation remedies as presented: **unverified/relevance unclear**. The earlier audit checked only the projection and streaming sentences; current wording now reflects those caveats.

### Engineering Practice (24)

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Dependency Inversion Principle.md
[[Dependency Inversion Principle|Dependency Inversion Principle]]
- **Accuracy:** **Partly supported, overbroad.** Constructor injection and explicit dependencies align with [Microsoft .NET DI guidelines, live/undated](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection-guidelines). “Depend on interfaces at all boundaries,” “every cross-layer collaborator injected via interface,” and “dependency arrows always point inward” describe one architecture style, not universal DIP requirements; definitions also conflate DIP with dependency injection.
- **Line-level accuracy update:** 28 candidates checked: 3 N/A, 6 Overbroad, 9 Partial, 5 Supported, 4 Unsupported, 1 Unverified. See claim-level checks for sources and corrected wording; these later verdicts supersede provisional accuracy wording above.
- **Detail:** Extensive examples; clearer contrast of principle, injection technique and where a concrete type is acceptable would improve it.
- **KB rules:** Properties/sections and links present. `Definition:` is a standalone label; verify following lines render as intended. Resources mostly bibliographic labels without URLs.
- **Location:** **Keep** — code-design principle, with links to application DI.
- **Actions:** Define DIP as high-level policy independent of low-level details; qualify interface/layer rules; source author and .NET examples.
- **Current gate:** **Not yet**.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Liskov Substitution Principle.md
[[Liskov Substitution Principle|Liskov Substitution Principle]]
- **Accuracy:** **Partly supported; absolute exception rule unsupported.** Behavioral contracts, invariants, pre/postconditions and history are in [Liskov & Wing, 1994 primary paper](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/barbara-liskov/behavioral-subtyping.pdf); initial keynote is [Liskov, ACM 1987](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/barbara-liskov/data-abstraction-and-hierarchy.pdf). Throwing `NotImplementedException` or `NotSupportedException` is a violation only if the supertype contract promised that operation for that input/state; “always/immediate” overstates it. “Contract testing at service boundary is LSP” is analogy, not identity.
- **Additional claim check:** 2 source lines: 2 Supported with condition. Direct evidence and proposed corrections are in Additional claim checks below.
- **Line-level accuracy update:** 22 candidates checked: 3 N/A, 2 Overbroad, 8 Partial, 5 Supported, 4 Unsupported. See claim-level checks for sources and corrected wording; these later verdicts supersede provisional accuracy wording above.
- **Detail:** Good conceptual detail and example categories; add explicit contract precondition to exception example.
- **KB rules:** Properties/sections and links present; original source bibliographic only.
- **Location:** **Keep** — code-design principle.
- **Actions:** Replace exception absolute with contract-conditioned rule; cite original paper.
- **Current gate:** **Not yet** until corrections and examples checked.

Each source line below is a claim candidate from the 2026-09-24 file snapshot. All 965 candidates received a second-pass verdict. `N/A` marks a heading, prompt, or other nonmaterial line; qualified support and partial verdicts name their limits. `Unverified-after-search` remains unresolved and does not qualify as `Current`. Original first-pass commentary remains for context; the **Second-pass evidence** is the later verdict where they differ. Primary source URLs are linked at the claim; all were accessed 2026-09-24. #### Areas/Foundations/Concurrency and Parallelism/Asynchronous Programming/Async.md — 23 reviewed claim candidates
- **L14 Partial:** **Definition:** Async/await is a structured way to model asynchronous work as awaitable operations, usually represented by tasks, futures, or promises, without blocking the current thread while the operation is incomplete. **Second-pass evidence:** [AS](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/async-in-depth). In C#, await suspends at an incomplete awaitable; genuinely asynchronous I/O need not hold a thread. Syntax alone cannot guarantee no blocking.
- **L17 Supported:** - I/O-bound work such as database calls, HTTP calls, file I/O, queue operations, or timers. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). Valid use cases if underlying APIs are asynchronous and concurrent work is bounded.
- **L18 Supported:** - UI or server code where blocked threads would reduce responsiveness or scalability. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). Valid use cases if underlying APIs are asynchronous and concurrent work is bounded.
- **L19 Supported:** - Independent operations that can be started together and awaited when their results are needed. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). Valid use cases if underlying APIs are asynchronous and concurrent work is bounded.
- **L25 Supported:** - Avoid `.Result`, `.Wait()`, and long synchronous work inside async flows. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). Prefer await to synchronous Result or Wait in async call paths.
- **L26 Partial:** - Use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in general-purpose library code when the continuation does not need the caller's context; app-level code usually does not need it. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). ConfigureAwait(false) is useful when a continuation need not capture context; library versus app is a contextual guideline.
- **L35 Supported:** Use async for waiting on external resources. Use parallelism for CPU-bound work that benefits from multiple cores. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). Async serves I/O waits; parallel execution serves suitable independent CPU work.
- **L38 Supported:** The common .NET shape is the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP): **Second-pass evidence:** [TAP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/task-based-asynchronous-pattern-tap). Scope to .NET TAP: Task without result, Task<T> with result, Async suffix by convention.
- **L40 Supported:** - `Task` represents an asynchronous operation with no result. **Second-pass evidence:** [TAP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/task-based-asynchronous-pattern-tap). Scope to .NET TAP: Task without result, Task<T> with result, Async suffix by convention.
- **L41 Supported:** - `Task<T>` represents an asynchronous operation that eventually produces a result. **Second-pass evidence:** [TAP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/task-based-asynchronous-pattern-tap). Scope to .NET TAP: Task without result, Task<T> with result, Async suffix by convention.
- **L42 Partial:** - `CancellationToken` lets callers request cancellation. **Second-pass evidence:** [CAN](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/task-cancellation). Expose/pass CancellationToken when operation supports it; cancellation is cooperative, not rollback.
- **L43 Partial:** - Exceptions are captured by the task and rethrown when awaited. **Second-pass evidence:** [AW](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/async). Exceptions from a Task-returning async method fault its task and surface on await; pre-return validation can throw synchronously.
- **L44 Supported:** - Methods returning awaitable types usually use the `Async` suffix. **Second-pass evidence:** [TAP](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/task-based-asynchronous-pattern-tap). Scope to .NET TAP: Task without result, Task<T> with result, Async suffix by convention.
- **L47 Supported:** A common mistake is awaiting each operation immediately when independent work could be started first. **Second-pass evidence:** [SC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). - **L54 Supported:** - Need unmatched rows from both sides (reconciliation): use FULL OUTER JOIN. **Second-pass evidence:** [primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/queries-table-expressions.html). FULL OUTER JOIN retains unmatched rows on both sides; reconcile by filtering missing keys.

#### Areas/Data Systems/Transactions and Concurrency/Transactions and Isolation Levels.md — 20 reviewed claim candidates
- **L14 Supported:** **Definition:** Transactions group database changes into reliable units of work, while isolation levels define how concurrent transactions can see and affect each other. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Transactions and isolation govern visibility and concurrent effects, subject to database implementation.
- **L17 Supported as use case:** - When preserving invariants across related reads and writes. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Related reads/writes can require transaction boundary and suitable isolation to protect invariants.
- **L18 Supported as use case:** - When debugging concurrency anomalies, locking, deadlocks, or inconsistent reads. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). Concurrency anomalies and deadlocks are documented transaction concerns.
- **L21 Supported with condition:** - Transactions protect correctness, but longer or broader transactions can reduce concurrency. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). Transactions support atomicity; long-held locks can reduce concurrency depending on implementation.
- **L22 Partial:** - Isolation is a tradeoff between stronger consistency and higher contention. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Stronger isolation can increase retries or locking overhead, but contention/performance is implementation-dependent; avoid a universal ordering.
- **L23 Supported as guidance:** - Know the anomalies you are trying to prevent before increasing isolation. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Choose isolation against anomalies the application must prevent; vendor behavior varies.
- **L31 Supported with condition:** - Atomicity: all changes in the transaction succeed or fail together. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html). Atomicity covers database changes in the transaction; external side effects are outside it absent coordinated protocol.
- **L32 Partial:** - Consistency: committed data should satisfy database and domain rules. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Database constraints are enforced at commit; domain rules require explicit implementation and correct isolation. Clarify consistency is not automatic domain correctness.
- **L33 Supported with condition:** - Isolation: concurrent transactions should not interfere beyond the chosen level. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Visibility and anomalies depend on selected isolation level; isolation is not absolute independence.
- **L34 Partial:** - Durability: committed changes survive failures according to the database guarantees. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-reliability.html). Durability depends on database configuration and documented commit guarantee; clarify scope instead of blanket crash survival.
- **L40 Supported:** | Dirty read | Reading uncommitted data from another transaction | **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Matches SQL isolation definition of dirty read.
- **L41 Supported:** | Non-repeatable read | Reading the same row twice and seeing different committed values | **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Matches SQL isolation definition of nonrepeatable read.
- **L42 Supported:** | Phantom read | Re-running a query and seeing new or removed rows | **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Matches SQL isolation definition of phantom read.
- **L43 Partial:** | Lost update | Concurrent writes overwrite each other without detection | **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Lost update is a concurrency anomaly, but preventability depends on update pattern and engine; define read-modify-write overwrite explicitly.
- **L44 Supported:** | Serializable behavior | Transactions behave as if they ran one at a time | **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Serializable means an effect equivalent to a serial order, not literally sequential execution.
- **L48 Supported as guidance:** - Keep transactions as short as the business operation allows. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). Shorter lock/transaction hold times usually reduce contention; business atomicity still controls boundary.
- **L49 Supported with condition:** - Use optimistic concurrency where conflicts are expected but uncommon. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Optimistic conflict handling suits workloads with infrequent conflict when retry semantics exist.
- **L50 Supported with condition:** - Use stronger locks or isolation when an invariant cannot tolerate races. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). Use locking or stronger isolation for a proven invariant race, taking engine behavior into account.
- **L51 Supported as guidance:** - Avoid doing slow external calls inside database transactions. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). External calls extend transaction duration and lock hold time; avoid when possible.
- **L52 Supported with condition:** - Log and retry deadlock or transient-concurrency failures only when the operation is safe to retry. **Second-pass evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). Retry serialization/deadlock failures after rollback when full operation is safe and idempotent; do not blindly retry side effects.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Interface Segregation Principle.md — 21 reviewed claim candidates
- **L15 Supported:** **Definition:** Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. - **L63 N/A:** - Caution: **Over-segregation:** One interface per method is impractical and produces dependency noise. **Second-pass evidence:** none. Anti-oversplitting design caution; no fixed evidence-based interface size.

- **L65 Supported:** - Caution: **Role interfaces vs header interfaces:** ISP favours role interfaces (defined by what the client needs) over header interfaces (a direct mirroring of a class's public surface). **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://objectmentor.com/resources/articles/isp.pdf). #### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Liskov Substitution Principle.md — 22 reviewed claim candidates
- **L18 N/A:** - Designing inheritance hierarchies or interface implementations. **Second-pass evidence:** none. Use-case prompts; no universal factual assertion.
- **L19 N/A:** - Validating that a new implementation truly satisfies a contract, not just its syntax. **Second-pass evidence:** none. Use-case prompts; no universal factual assertion.
- **L22 Supported:** - Subclasses must honour the **behavioural contract** of the base type, not just compile against its signature. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Behavioral subtyping requires properties expected of the supertype to remain valid.
- **L24 Unsupported:** - `NotImplementedException` in an override is an immediate LSP violation. **Checked clause/correction:** Only a violation when the supertype contract promises the operation for that input/state. [Primary source](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/barbara-liskov/behavioral-subtyping.pdf). **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). An exception violates substitutability only where it breaches a promised supertype behavior for that state/input.
- **L25 N/A:** - Prefer composition over inheritance when a subtype cannot fully substitute the base. **Second-pass evidence:** none. Design recommendation; composition is one option when the proposed subtype contract fails.
- **L78 Supported:** - Caution: **Syntactic vs behavioural conformance:** A class can compile as a subtype while violating invariants the base type's callers depend on. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Syntactic subtype conformance alone does not establish behavioral substitutability.
- **L79 Unsupported:** - Caution: **Throwing in overrides:** Throwing `NotSupportedException` or `NotImplementedException` in an inherited method is always an LSP violation. **Checked clause/correction:** “Always” is false without checking the supertype contract; qualify by promised behavior. [Primary source](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/barbara-liskov/behavioral-subtyping.pdf). **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). An exception violates substitutability only where it breaches a promised supertype behavior for that state/input.
- **L80 Partial:** - Caution: **Interface bloat causing LSP pressure:** Large interfaces force implementations to fake methods — prefer small interfaces ([[Interface Segregation Principle]]). **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://objectmentor.com/resources/articles/isp.pdf). Fat interfaces can pressure fake implementations, but size alone does not prove an LSP breach.
- **L87 Partial:** Barbara Liskov introduced this principle in her 1987 keynote. The formal definition involves **behavioural subtyping**: a type `S` is a subtype of `T` if every property provable about `T` objects is also provable about `S` objects. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Behavioral-subtyping formulation is supported; the 1987 keynote attribution needs a separate original program/source.
- **L90 Supported:** - **Invariants** established by the base type must be preserved. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Invariant and pre/postcondition constraints follow the behavioral subtyping formulation, subject to stated supertype contract.
- **L91 Supported:** - **Preconditions** (what callers must guarantee) cannot be made stricter in the subtype. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Invariant and pre/postcondition constraints follow the behavioral subtyping formulation, subject to stated supertype contract.
- **L92 Supported:** - **Postconditions** (what the method guarantees to callers) cannot be weakened. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Invariant and pre/postcondition constraints follow the behavioral subtyping formulation, subject to stated supertype contract.
- **L93 Partial:** - **History constraint:** subtype methods must not introduce side effects the base type would prohibit. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). History constraints concern observable behavior allowed by the supertype, not every side effect.
- **L98 Partial:** | Throws in override | Override throws where base never would | **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). These are violation signals only if they contradict the base contract, not automatically.
- **L99 Unsupported:** | Narrowed return range | Returns subset of values the base contract advertises | **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). A subtype returning a valid subset of the advertised range may strengthen, not weaken, the postcondition.
- **L100 Partial:** | Ignored method | Override does nothing (e.g. `void Save() {}`) | **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). These are violation signals only if they contradict the base contract, not automatically.
- **L101 Partial:** | Strengthened precondition | Subtype demands more from callers than base | **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). These are violation signals only if they contradict the base contract, not automatically.
- **L102 Partial:** | Classic Rectangle/Square | Geometry doesn't map to IS-A; mutability breaks invariants | **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). - **L105 Overbroad:** - LSP makes **OCP** safe — if subtypes aren't substitutable, extending via polymorphism breaks correctness. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). LSP supports safe polymorphic extension; ISP does not guarantee LSP or become a strict prerequisite.
- **L106 Overbroad:** - **ISP** prevents LSP violations by keeping interfaces small enough that no implementor needs to fake a method. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). - **L110 Partial:** Ask: "Can I replace every instance of the base type with this subtype and have the system still behave correctly?" If not, reconsider the inheritance relationship. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~wing/publications/LiskovWing94.pdf). Use behavioral contract preservation, not literal replacement in every program context, as the test.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Open-Closed Principle.md — 22 reviewed claim candidates
- **L15 Partial:** **Definition:** Software entities should be **open for extension** but **closed for modification** — add new behaviour by adding new code, not by changing existing code. **Second-pass evidence:** [source](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/05/12/TheOpenClosedPrinciple.html). OCP seeks extension without changing protected code; “add new code, never change existing” is too absolute.

#### Areas/Foundations/Concurrency and Parallelism/Asynchronous Programming/Async.md

- **L22 Supported:** - Async is about non-blocking waiting; it is not automatically parallel execution. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). **Assessment/change:** Async I/O can yield without occupying a worker; CPU parallelism is separate.
- **L23 Supported:** - In .NET, `async` enables `await`, but the method runs synchronously until it reaches an incomplete awaitable. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios). **Assessment/change:** Async method executes before first incomplete await; method may complete synchronously.
- **L24 Supported with condition:** - Prefer `Task`/`Task<T>` for most .NET async APIs; use `ValueTask` only when measurement shows it helps and callers can handle its constraints. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.valuetask-1). **Assessment/change:** Task is conventional default; ValueTask benefit depends on allocation profile and single-consumption constraints.

#### Areas/Foundations/Concurrency and Parallelism/Concurrent Patterns/Thread Pool.md

- **L15 Supported:** **Definition:** A thread pool reuses a managed set of worker threads to execute queued work without creating and destroying a dedicated thread for every operation. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool). **Assessment/change:** Managed worker threads are reused for queued tasks; pool can also create or retire threads dynamically.

#### Areas/Foundations/Programming Concepts/Programming Paradigms/Inheritance.md

- **L30 Supported with condition:** - Caution: C# enforces **single inheritance** (one base class); implement multiple interfaces for broader composition. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/object-oriented/inheritance). **Assessment/change:** C# class inheritance is single-base; multiple interfaces may be implemented. Interfaces are contracts, not composition by themselves.

#### Areas/Foundations/Programming Concepts/Programming Paradigms/Polymorphism.md

- **L15 Supported with condition:** **Definition:** The ability for objects of different types to be treated through a common interface; enables writing code that works with abstractions instead of concrete types. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/object-oriented/polymorphism). **Assessment/change:** C# polymorphism can use base classes/interfaces; common-interface wording is narrower than all polymorphism.
- **L30 Partial:** - [[Liskov Substitution Principle|LSP]] guarantees that derived types can safely substitute base types. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/barbara-liskov/behavioral-subtyping.pdf). **Assessment/change:** LSP states a required behavioral substitutability relation; inheritance alone does not guarantee that derived types satisfy it.

Source line: Definition: Cell-based architecture partitions a system into isolated cells, where each cell contains the services and data needed to serve a subset of users, tenants, or traffic.
- **L17 Supported:** - Large-scale platforms that need blast-radius reduction, tenant isolation, regional isolation, or controlled horizontal growth. **Evidence:** [A1](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/wellarchitected/latest/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture.pdf). **Assessment/change:** Cell isolation and routing can limit the impact of a fault to one partition, subject to shared dependencies. - **L19 Partial:** - Any codebase where testability and explicit dependencies matter. **Evidence:** [primary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines). **Assessment/change:** Microsoft advises against runtime service lookup when injection suffices; late registration and test friction are risks, not certainties. - **L22 Supported:** - Avoid: Hides true dependencies from constructors and APIs. **Evidence:** [A10](https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/injection.html). **Assessment/change:** Ambient lookup hides dependency requirements from method or constructor signatures. - **L23 Partial:** - Avoid: Makes unit tests harder because hidden collaborators must be configured globally. **Evidence:** [primary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/guidelines). **Assessment/change:** Microsoft advises against runtime service lookup when injection suffices; late registration and test friction are risks, not certainties. #### Areas/Architecture and System Design/Integration and Messaging/Event-Driven Integration/Event-Driven Architecture.md

- **L13 Supported:** **Definition:** An architecture in which producers publish events about changes and consumers react to those events, often asynchronously. **Evidence:** [A5](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven). **Assessment/change:** Event producers emit facts and consumers react, often asynchronously. Source line: Definition: An architecture in which producers publish events about changes and consumers react to those events, often asynchronously.
- **L16 Partial:** - Systems needing high decoupling, asynchronous processing, or event-sourced patterns. **Evidence:** [A5](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven). **Assessment/change:** Event sourcing is optional; scalability and eventual consistency depend on channel and state-update design. Source line: Systems needing high decoupling, asynchronous processing, or event-sourced patterns.
- **L19 Partial:** - **Loose coupling** and improved scalability. **Evidence:** [A5](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven). **Assessment/change:** Event sourcing is optional; scalability and eventual consistency depend on channel and state-update design. - **L20 Partial:** - **Eventual consistency** and operational complexity require explicit handling. **Evidence:** [A5](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven). **Assessment/change:** Event sourcing is optional; scalability and eventual consistency depend on channel and state-update design. #### Areas/Architecture and System Design/Integration and Messaging/Integration Styles/API Gateway Pattern.md

- **L14 Supported:** **Definition:** An API gateway is an edge component that provides a single entry point to backend services, often handling routing, authentication, rate limiting, protocol translation, or cross-cutting API concerns. **Evidence:** [A6](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/design/gateway). **Assessment/change:** Gateway can provide edge entry, routing, policy, translation and observation. Source line: Definition: An API gateway is an edge component that provides a single entry point to backend services, often handling routing, authentication, rate limiting, protocol translation,
- **L17 Supported:** - When clients need a stable entry point in front of multiple backend services. **Evidence:** [A6](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/design/gateway). **Assessment/change:** Gateway can provide edge entry, routing, policy, translation and observation. Source line: When clients need a stable entry point in front of multiple backend services.
- **L18 Supported:** - When cross-cutting edge concerns should be centralized without duplicating them in every service. **Evidence:** [A6](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/microservices/design/gateway). **Assessment/change:** Gateway can provide edge entry, routing, policy, translation and observation. - **L17 Supported:** - When web, mobile, partner, or internal clients need different API shapes, aggregation, auth flows, or performance tradeoffs. **Evidence:** [A7](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/backends-for-frontends). **Assessment/change:** BFF tailors a backend contract to a client experience and may aggregate data. #### Areas/Architecture and System Design/Integration and Messaging/Integration Styles/Message-Driven Architecture.md

- **L14 Supported:** **Definition:** Message-driven architecture coordinates work through messages such as commands, events, and documents sent over queues, topics, streams, or brokers. **Evidence:** [A18](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/multi-container-microservice-net-applications/integration-event-based-microservice-communications). **Assessment/change:** Queues/topics can decouple producers and consumers in time and carry commands/events. Source line: Definition: Message-driven architecture coordinates work through messages such as commands, events, and documents sent over queues, topics, streams, or brokers.
- **L17 Supported:** - When producers and consumers should be decoupled in time, availability, or throughput. **Evidence:** [A18](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/multi-container-microservice-net-applications/integration-event-based-microservice-communications). **Assessment/change:** Queues/topics can decouple producers and consumers in time and carry commands/events. Source line: When producers and consumers should be decoupled in time, availability, or throughput.
- **L18 Supported:** - When background processing, retries, buffering, or fan-out is more appropriate than synchronous calls. **Evidence:** [A18](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/microservices/multi-container-microservice-net-applications/integration-event-based-microservice-communications). **Assessment/change:** Queues/topics can decouple producers and consumers in time and carry commands/events. Source line: When background processing, retries, buffering, or fan-out is more appropriate than synchronous calls.

#### Areas/State, Coordination and Workflows/Workflow and Long-Running Processes/Sagas/Saga Pattern.md

- **L21 Partial:** - Sagas replace atomic cross-service transactions with explicit workflow state and compensation. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Saga local transactions plus compensation do not provide global atomicity; say 'sagas coordinate eventual consistency where distributed atomic transaction is not used'.
- **L23 Supported:** - Compensation is business logic, not a simple technical rollback. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Compensation reverses business effects with new local actions; it is not database rollback. Clarify irreversibility/pivot cases.
- **L33 Partial:** | Orchestration | A coordinator tells participants what to do next | Complex workflows needing visibility and control | Coordinator can become a god service | **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Orchestrator centralizes decisions/state; 'god service' is a possible design failure, not inherent. State as risk of excessive responsibility.
- **L34 Partial:** | Choreography | Services react to events and publish their own events | Simple, loosely coupled flows | Workflow becomes hard to see and debug | **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Choreography uses events and can be harder to trace as steps grow; 'simple flows' is guidance, not universal threshold.
- **L39 Partial:** - Make each step idempotent. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Retryable saga steps need idempotency, but not every compensable step is intrinsically idempotent. Say design retryable commands/compensations for duplicate delivery.
- **L40 Partial:** - Define compensation for business failures, not only technical failures. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Compensation may be needed for business/technical failure after committed local steps; line's 'not only technical' is useful but does not define all failure handling.
- **L47 Partial:** - The workflow requires immediate global consistency. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** Immediate global consistency is not what a saga's eventually consistent sequence guarantees; prefer a transaction/coordination mechanism matching required invariant.
- **L48 Supported:** - The business cannot define safe compensating actions. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga). **Assessment/change:** If effects cannot be compensated or made forward-recoverable, the saga design needs a pivot/retry strategy or a different boundary.

#### Areas/Cloud and Platform Engineering/Platform Engineering/Service Mesh.md

- **L14 Supported with condition:** **Definition:** A service mesh moves service-to-service networking concerns such as traffic policy, mutual TLS, retries, telemetry, and routing into a dedicated infrastructure layer, often through sidecars or node-level proxies. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Istio documents mesh traffic/security/telemetry, but not all meshes use same infrastructure architecture.
- **L17 Partial:** - When a microservice platform needs consistent service-to-service security, traffic control, and observability. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Use when the same service traffic and identity policies recur across workloads; the overview shows capability, not that a mesh is warranted for every platform.
- **L18 N/A:** - When these concerns are too important or duplicated to leave inside every service codebase. **Evidence:** none. **Assessment/change:** Example label, process instruction or contextual design prompt; no independent vendor fact to verify.
- **L21 Partial:** - A service mesh is platform infrastructure, not an architecture cure-all. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Keep as a limitation: a mesh handles selected network concerns, while service design, failure handling and data consistency still need application decisions.
- **L22 Partial:** - It can standardize cross-cutting networking concerns but adds operational complexity. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** The official overview supports traffic and security features; add a concrete control-plane/configuration cost and measure it for the platform.
- **L23 N/A:** - Teams should understand the underlying failure modes, not hide all networking behind mesh configuration. **Evidence:** none. **Assessment/change:** Example label, process instruction or contextual design prompt; no independent vendor fact to verify.
- **L31 Partial:** - Mutual TLS between services. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Istio supports mTLS, but effective enforcement depends on PeerAuthentication/TLS configuration; link the official TLS configuration guide.
- **L32 Partial:** - Traffic splitting, routing, retries, and timeouts. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Istio documents routing, retries and timeouts; warn that retry safety and timeout budgets depend on operation semantics.
- **L33 Partial:** - Service-to-service metrics, traces, and logs. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Istio emits telemetry, but logs/traces/metrics require deployment and instrumentation choices; specify which signals are actually available.
- **L34 Partial:** - Policy enforcement and identity-aware communication. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Istio policy and workload identity are configurable; name the relevant authorization and identity policy rather than implying universal enforcement.
- **L38 Partial:** - Many services with common networking and security requirements. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** This is a selection heuristic, not a product fact. State the repeated cross-service requirement and compare mesh cost with simpler ingress/library policies.
- **L39 Partial:** - Mature platform teams operating Kubernetes or similar orchestration. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** This is an adoption judgment; spell out who owns the control plane, upgrades, incident response and policy rollout.
- **L40 Partial:** - Need for consistent telemetry and traffic policy across services. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** A mesh can centralize traffic/telemetry configuration; validate the platform and data collection setup before promising consistency.
- **L44 Partial:** - The estate is small enough that simpler platform defaults are enough. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** This is a tradeoff recommendation. Give a small-estate example where ingress, client libraries or platform defaults cover the requirements.
- **L45 Partial:** - The team lacks operational ownership for the mesh control plane. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Operational ownership is a valid adoption limit; assign an owner for control-plane upgrades, policy changes and incidents.
- **L46 Partial:** - Retry and timeout policies are applied without understanding application semantics. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/). **Assessment/change:** Retries can repeat non-idempotent calls or amplify load; define operation-specific retry and timeout budgets before configuring mesh policy.

- **L19 Partial:** - When evolving code with confidence in regression protection. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices). **Assessment/change:** Tests can catch regressions but only for covered behavior and reliable assertions; 'confidence' is contingent.
- **L23 Partial:** - The red-green-refactor cycle encourages small, composable changes. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html). **Assessment/change:** Red-green-refactor encourages small steps; 'composable changes' is design judgment, not inevitable outcome.
- **L24 Supported:** - Caution: Weak test design can lock in brittle implementations. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices). **Assessment/change:** Poorly designed tests can be brittle and constrain refactoring; give behavior-focused example.
- **L37 Partial:** - API shape and object boundaries often emerge from the test seams. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDrivenDevelopment.html). **Assessment/change:** Tests can influence API seams/design; 'often emerge' frequency is unverified. Recast as possible technique.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Liskov Substitution Principle.md

- **L15 Supported with condition:** **Definition:** Objects of a subtype must be substitutable for objects of their supertype without altering the correctness of the program. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/barbara-liskov/behavioral-subtyping.pdf). **Assessment/change:** Substitutability is behavioral and relative to the supertype contract, not merely type inheritance.
- **L23 Supported with condition:** - Preconditions cannot be strengthened; postconditions cannot be weakened. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.cs.tufts.edu/comp/150FP/archive/barbara-liskov/behavioral-subtyping.pdf). **Assessment/change:** Subtypes may not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions under the stated behavioral contract.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Design and Construction/Single Responsibility Principle.md

- **L23 Supported with condition:** - "Reason to change" = a stakeholder or actor whose requirements drive that code. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://blog.cleancoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/05/08/SingleReponsibilityPrinciple.html). **Assessment/change:** Original author frames reason to change as a stakeholder actor; treat as design heuristic, not mathematical identity.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Code Review/Code Review Guidelines.md

- **L21 Supported as guidance:** - **Keep reviews small:** Smaller PRs reduce cognitive load and speed up reviews. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html). **Assessment/change:** Google review guidance favors small changes for review speed; no universal size threshold.

#### Areas/Engineering Practice/Developer Tooling/AI-Assisted Development.md

- **L21 Supported as guidance:** - Treat AI output as a proposal, not an authority. Review, test, and validate generated code. **Evidence:** [Primary source](https://www.nist.gov/publications/artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence). **Assessment/change:** Human oversight/validation are risk controls; specific test policy is local engineering guidance.

#### Areas/Languages, Runtimes and Frameworks/Frameworks and Platforms/DotNET/ASP.NET Core/APIs/ASP.NET Core Integration Testing.md

- **L13 Supported:** **Definition:** Integration testing verifies how ASP.NET Core components work together across real application boundaries. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Integration tests verify cooperation of app components and may include infrastructure and request processing. Replace 'real application boundaries' with 'application composition and selected infrastructure'; tests may substitute dependencies.
- **L16 Supported:** - When testing routing, middleware, dependency wiring, persistence boundaries, or HTTP behaviour. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Routing/request pipeline and configured services fit documented integration-test scope. Persistence tests need an intentionally chosen test data store or substitute; HTTP behavior is exercised via test client.
- **L19 Partial:** - Exercise the host through public behaviour, not internal implementation details. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Testing observable HTTP responses is illustrated, but 'not internal implementation details' is a design preference rather than a prohibition. State as recommendation.
- **L20 Partial:** - Keep external dependencies deterministic and isolated for repeatable tests. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Microsoft demonstrates test-specific databases and service overrides. Deterministic isolation requires explicit seeding, cleanup and external-dependency control; the test host alone does not provide it.
- **L25 Supported:** Use an application test host with controlled configuration and dependencies. Keep fast unit tests for isolated logic; use integration tests for behaviour that depends on the application composition. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/integration-tests?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** WebApplicationFactory/TestServer host an app with configurable services/settings. Separate unit tests for isolated logic and integration tests for composition follows the guide's stated scope.

#### Areas/Languages, Runtimes and Frameworks/Frameworks and Platforms/DotNET/ASP.NET Core/Configuration/ASP.NET Core Options Pattern.md

- **L14 Supported:** **Definition:** The options pattern binds configuration to typed .NET objects and injects those objects into application services. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Options bind configuration sections to typed classes and are consumed through injected IOptions abstractions. Specify that injection is of an options wrapper, rather than necessarily direct injection of the object.
- **L17 Partial:** - When configuration has a stable named shape and consumers benefit from typed access. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Typed options suit related settings in a section. 'Stable named shape' is design judgment, not a requirement; named options are optional and distinct from merely using a section.
- **L20 Partial:** - Bind and validate options at the application boundary. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Binding and validation are available, but validation does not automatically run at startup. Recommend ValidateOnStart when startup failure is required; default validation occurs when an options instance is first created/accessed.
- **L21 Supported:** - Choose the options interface that matches the required lifetime and reload semantics. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** IOptions is singleton without reload, IOptionsSnapshot is scoped/per-request, and IOptionsMonitor is singleton with reload/change notifications. Reload depends on a provider that supplies updates.
- **L26 Partial:** Register a configuration section with Configure<TOptions> and inject the appropriate options abstraction into the consumer. Keep configuration types focused on the external configuration contract; avoid passing raw configuration access throughout the application. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/options?view=aspnetcore-10.0). **Assessment/change:** Configure<TOptions>(section) registers binding and IOptions abstractions can be injected. A focused options class and avoiding raw IConfiguration in consumers are reasonable design guidance, not framework mandates; validation needs separate registration.

#### Areas/Languages, Runtimes and Frameworks/Languages/CSharp/Language Fundamentals/CSharp Fundamentals.md

- **L21 Partial:** - Learn collection and LINQ tradeoffs early because they shape day-to-day implementation quality. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/). **Assessment/change:** Collection choices alter access patterns and safety; LINQ choice can affect execution. 'Learn early' and quality ranking are editorial. Reword as recommended study sequence, not measured priority.
- **L29 Partial:** 1. **Types and contracts**: understand nullability and generics first. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references). **Assessment/change:** Nullable annotations describe null contracts; generics/constraints describe type capabilities. 'First' is an editorial learning order, not a prerequisite for every C# task.
- **L30 Supported:** 2. **Behavior as data**: learn delegates, `Func<>`, and events. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/delegates/using-delegates). **Assessment/change:** Delegates are typed references to callable methods; Func is a generic delegate family; events use delegates for notifications. 'Behavior as data' is a useful analogy, not a formal definition.
- **L31 Partial:** 3. **Data manipulation**: learn collection choices before building heavy LINQ habits. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/selecting-a-collection-class). **Assessment/change:** Collection type selection can affect complexity and behavior; learning collections before LINQ is an editorial sequence, not a language requirement.
- **L32 Partial:** 4. **Querying and transformation**: use LINQ once you understand source collection behavior and execution models. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/). **Assessment/change:** LINQ query operators work over source sequences and can defer execution; provider behavior varies for IQueryable. Prior collection study is advice, not a requirement.
- **L35 Supported:** - [[Access Modifiers]] - Visibility boundaries for maintainable APIs and encapsulation. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/access-modifiers). **Assessment/change:** Access modifiers constrain where types and members can be used. 'Maintainable APIs/encapsulation' is design rationale, not guaranteed by modifier selection.
- **L36 Supported:** - [[Nullable Reference Types]] - Null-safety contracts, annotations, and migration guidance. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references). **Assessment/change:** Nullable reference annotations plus flow analysis express null contracts and compiler warnings; they do not add runtime null enforcement.
- **L37 Partial:** - [[Generic Constraints]] - Type-safe reuse, constraints, and variance basics. **Evidence:** [constraints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/generics/constraints-on-type-parameters), [variance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/generics/covariance-and-contravariance). **Assessment/change:** Generic constraints support typed operations. Variance is a related generic topic but distinct from constraints; keep description broad or link variance separately.
- **L38 Supported:** - [[Delegates, Events, and Actions]] - Passing behavior, callbacks, and event-driven design at the language level. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/delegates/using-delegates). **Assessment/change:** Delegates support passing callable behavior and callbacks; event declarations use delegate types for notification.
- **L39 Supported:** - [[Collection Types]] - Choosing the right in-memory data structure and API contract. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/selecting-a-collection-class). **Assessment/change:** Collection classes have different behavior and performance; public API contract should match intended operations. No collection is universally best.
- **L40 Partial:** - [[Immutable and Concurrent Collections]] - When read-only is not enough and shared state needs stronger guarantees. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/thread-safe/). **Assessment/change:** Concurrent collections support safe simultaneous updates; immutable collections prevent mutation of existing instances. Read-only interfaces alone do not imply immutability or synchronized writes.
- **L41 Partial:** - [[LINQ]] - Declarative querying, projection, deferred execution, and provider translation. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/). **Assessment/change:** LINQ offers query operators and projection; many IEnumerable operators defer execution. Provider translation concerns IQueryable sources and is provider-dependent, not a property of all LINQ.
- **L44 Supported:** - Nullability and generics shape safe API surfaces. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references). **Assessment/change:** Nullability annotations express allowed null states; generic type parameters/constraints express allowed types and operations. 'Safe' still depends on runtime checks and implementation.
- **L45 Partial:** - Delegates power LINQ and many framework callback patterns. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions). **Assessment/change:** Enumerable LINQ operators commonly take Func delegates. Queryable operators use expression trees typed Expression<Func<...>>; 'delegates power LINQ' is too broad. Say delegates power LINQ to Objects while query providers often use expression trees.
- **L46 Supported:** - Collection choice influences LINQ performance, allocation, and semantics. **Evidence:** [collections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/), [LINQ operators](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/linq/standard-query-operators/). **Assessment/change:** Collection properties can affect iteration cost and resulting LINQ behavior; allocation/performance varies by operator, source and provider. Avoid a blanket direction or magnitude.
- **L47 Partial:** - Immutable and concurrent collections are specialized responses to ownership and threading concerns. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/thread-safe/). **Assessment/change:** Immutable and concurrent collections address different shared-state concerns. Immutability can simplify sharing; concurrent collections coordinate mutations. Choice depends on ownership and write patterns.
- **L63 Supported:** 2. Build a tiny sample that combines `List<T>`, `Func<T, bool>`, and LINQ, then refactor the public API to use better abstractions. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/lambda-expressions). **Assessment/change:** List<T> can be queried with LINQ, and a Func<T,bool> can be passed to delegate-taking Enumerable operators. The proposed refactor is an exercise, not evidence of a universally better API.
- **L64 Partial:** 3. Review one API surface and decide whether it should expose mutable collections, read-only interfaces, or immutable data. **Evidence:** [primary source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/). **Assessment/change:** Mutable, read-only and immutable collection contracts expose different mutation guarantees. A read-only interface may wrap mutable state, so use true immutable data or a defensive copy if callers require a stable snapshot.
